{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-orthogonal-perpendicular}
#### Orthogonal means perpendicular

Orthogonality extends the geometric idea of perpendicular lines
to vectors with any number of entries.
In the plane, $(1, 2)$ and $(-2, 1)$ are perpendicular,
and their dot product is $1 \cd (-2) + 2 \cd 1 = 0$.
The same test works in $\reals^3$, where pictures are harder to draw:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1, 1, 0) \cdot (1, -1, 5) &= 1 - 1 + 0 \\
&= 0,
\end{aligned}
$$

so $(1, 1, 0) \perp (1, -1, 5)$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-not-orthogonal}
#### Vectors that are not orthogonal

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1, 2) \cdot (1, 1) &= 1 \cd 1 + 2 \cd 1 \\
&= 3 \\
&\ne 0,
\end{aligned}
$$

so $(1, 2)$ and $(1, 1)$ are not orthogonal.

:::
